questions.q: Which of these is the World Health Organization (WHO) definition of health given in the chapter?
o: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease
A state of complete physical fitness and strength, with freedom from every kind of pain and illness at all times
A state in which a person has no disease of the body or of the mind at any time
A state of physical and mental well-being in which a person never falls sick at all
questions.a: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease.

questions.q: Four Class 8 students are described below. Which one is healthy in the sense the WHO uses?
o: Gita has no illness, stays positive and gets along well with her classmates and family
Hari is the fastest runner in school but quarrels with everyone and eats lunch alone
Lata has many friends and is cheerful, but she has had a high fever for five days
Manoj has no illness and plays cricket daily, but he feels worried and low most of the time
questions.a: Gita: she is well in body (no illness), in mind (stays positive) and socially (gets along with others), which covers all three aspects of the WHO definition.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Health and happiness are closely related.
Reason (R): Being happy helps us stay active and healthy, and good health also improves our mood.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: happiness helps us stay healthy and good health improves our mood, so each supports the other.

questions.q:
Read the statements about health.
Statement I: A healthy person can generally perform various tasks more efficiently.
Statement II: According to the WHO, a person who has no disease is completely healthy.
Statement III: A healthy person can cope well in different and difficult situations.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the WHO says health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease.

questions.q:
(a) Name the three aspects of health that make up the WHO definition.
(b) According to the same definition, health is not merely the absence of what?
questions.a: (a) Physical, mental and social well-being. (b) Disease: health is not merely the absence of disease.
s: (a) all three aspects named: physical, mental and social
(b) the absence of disease

questions.q: True or False: The WHO definition of health is about the body and the mind only; how well a person gets along with other people is not part of it. Give the verdict and correct the statement if needed.
questions.a: False. The WHO definition also includes social well-being: a healthy person can adjust well with peer groups and other members of society.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: social well-being (adjusting well with peer groups and society) is one of the three aspects of health

questions.q:
Dhruv plays football every evening and has not fallen ill all year. In group projects he refuses to listen to anyone else's ideas and argues until the group breaks up, so his classmates now avoid working with him.
(a) Which aspect of health do his problems with his group show is weak?
(b) Using the WHO definition, decide whether Dhruv is completely healthy and give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Social well-being: he does not adjust well with his peer group. (b) He is not completely healthy: the WHO definition needs physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease, so being fit and free of illness is not enough.
s: (a) social well-being, as he does not adjust well with his peer group
(b) not completely healthy, because health needs social well-being too and is not merely the absence of disease

questions.q:
According to the chapter, a healthy person can do three things better. State what the chapter says a healthy person can do:
(a) with the tasks he or she has to do,
(b) in different and difficult situations,
(c) with peer groups and other members of society.
questions.a: (a) A healthy person can generally perform various tasks more efficiently. (b) A healthy person can cope well in different and difficult situations. (c) A healthy person can adjust well with peer groups and other members of society.
s: (a) performs various tasks more efficiently
(b) copes well in different and difficult situations
(c) adjusts well with peer groups and other members of society

questions.q:
Ms Lyngdoh, a class teacher in Shillong, writes short notes on four Class 8 students after a week.
Neha: no illness and has many friends, but feels anxious and cries before every test.
Tenzin: cheerful and popular, but has sprained his ankle and walks on crutches.
Sara: no illness and stays positive, but sits alone at lunch and talks to no one.
Imon: no illness, cheerful, and plays and studies with his friends every day.
(a) Which student is healthy in all three aspects of health?
(b) Which aspect of health is affected for Tenzin?
(c) Which aspect is weak for Neha, and which for Sara?
(d) Sara's father says, 'She has no disease, so she is perfectly healthy.' Is he right? Give a reason from the WHO definition.
questions.a: (a) Imon. (b) Physical well-being (the sprained ankle). (c) Neha: mental well-being; Sara: social well-being. (d) No: the WHO says health is complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease; Sara's social well-being is weak.
s: (a) Imon
(b) physical well-being
(c) Neha mental, Sara social well-being
(d) not right: health is not merely the absence of disease, and her social well-being is weak

questions.q:
A fitness app gives each user a 'Health Score' out of 30, using three numbers only: daily steps (up to 10 points), body weight in the healthy range (up to 10 points) and days without falling sick in the last month (up to 10 points). Two users:
Priya: 12,000 steps a day, healthy weight, no sick days; score 30. She says she has no one to talk to and feels low most evenings.
Qasim: 7,000 steps a day, healthy weight, 2 sick days with a cold; score 24. He is cheerful and spends time with friends and family.
(a) Which aspect of health does the app's score measure?
(b) Name the two aspects of the WHO definition it leaves out.
(c) Suggest one question the app could ask to check each missing aspect.
(d) The app calls Priya 'the healthiest user'. Judge this title, comparing Priya and Qasim on all three aspects.
questions.a: (a) Physical well-being only (steps, weight and days without sickness). (b) Mental well-being and social well-being. (c) Mental: for example, 'How often do you feel positive, and how often low?'; social: 'Do you have friends or family you talk to and get along with?' (d) The title is not deserved. Priya is best physically, but she feels low and has no one to talk to, so her mental and social well-being are weak. Qasim is a little behind physically (fewer steps, a cold) but is cheerful and has strong relationships. By the WHO definition, complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease, Qasim is closer to complete health; Priya needs support for her mind and relationships.
s: (a) physical well-being only
(b) mental and social well-being
(c) one sensible check for mental and one for social well-being
(d) Priya's mental and social well-being are weak although she is best physically; Qasim is strong on both
(d) judgement: the title is not deserved, as by the WHO definition Qasim is closer to complete health

questions.q: When we are unwell, which of these is a sign of illness rather than a symptom?
questions.a: High blood pressure: a sign is something that can be seen or measured, while pain, tiredness and dizziness are symptoms, which are what we feel.

questions.q: What does the Air Quality Index (AQI) help us know?
o: How much rain will fall in a city
How many people in a city have asthma
How clean the drinking water is
questions.a: How clean the air is.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with what the chapter says about it in Column II.
Column I: 1. Air pollution from vehicles and factories  2. The Air Quality Index  3. Getting enough sleep  4. Spending time with friends and family
Column II: A. Helps the body and mind rest and recover  B. Can cause problems like coughing or asthma  C. Helps keep our minds healthy  D. Helps us know how clean the air is
questions.a: 1-B, 2-D, 3-A, 4-C: polluted air can cause coughing or asthma; the AQI tells how clean the air is; sleep lets the body and mind rest and recover; time with friends and family keeps the mind healthy.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): People living near a dirty playground full of flies and mosquitoes may fall sick more often.
Reason (R): A symptom is something that can be seen or measured, like a rash.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. A polluted, unhygienic place full of flies and mosquitoes can make people fall sick more often. R is false: a symptom is what we feel (like pain); a sign is what can be seen or measured (like a rash or fever).

questions.q: Differentiate between a symptom and a sign of illness, giving one example of each.
questions.a: A symptom is what we feel, for example pain, tiredness or dizziness. A sign is something that can be seen or measured, for example fever (high body temperature), rash, high blood pressure or swelling.
s: Symptom: what we feel, with one example (pain / tiredness / dizziness)
Sign: what can be seen or measured, with one example (fever / rash / high blood pressure / swelling)

questions.q:
Sahil runs every morning and never eats junk food, but he plays games on his phone until 1 a.m. and sleeps only five hours a night. He says, 'I exercise and eat well, so my late nights cannot matter.'
(a) Name the two pieces of healthy-lifestyle advice in the chapter that his nights go against.
(b) Using what the chapter says sleep does, explain why exercise and diet cannot make up for them.
questions.a: (a) Limit screen time, and get enough sleep. (b) The chapter says we need enough sleep to help the body and mind rest and recover; running and good food do not give that rest, so his late nights still harm his health.
s: (a) limit screen time and get enough sleep
(b) sleep lets the body and mind rest and recover, which exercise and diet do not provide

questions.q:
Answer from the chapter's advice for a healthy lifestyle.
(a) Which kinds of food and drink should we avoid?
(b) Name any two harmful substances to which we should say 'No'.
(c) Name the simple breathing exercise the chapter suggests practising regularly.
questions.a: (a) Processed, fatty or sugary food and drinks. (b) Any two of tobacco, alcohol and addictive drugs. (c) Pranayama.
s: (a) processed, fatty or sugary food and drinks
(b) any two of tobacco, alcohol, addictive drugs
(c) pranayama

questions.q: A gym in Pune puts up a banner: 'Build a strong body and you will be completely healthy.' Is the claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Staying physically active is part of a healthy lifestyle and helps the body. But a strong body alone is not complete health: we also need a balanced diet, enough sleep and a clean environment (polluted air can cause coughing or asthma), and the chapter says that even if we eat well and live in a clean place we may not feel good if we are lonely or upset, so feelings and relationships matter too.
s: Verdict: partly right, accepting exercise as part of a healthy lifestyle
Other lifestyle and environment factors are also needed (diet, sleep, clean air or surroundings)
Feelings and relationships also matter: a person may not feel good if lonely or upset

questions.q:
A school beside a busy road in Ghaziabad records sick-room visits for coughing. On five days when the AQI display showed poor air, the visits were 18, 22, 25, 20 and 15. On five days when it showed good air, they were 4, 3, 5, 2 and 6. The students followed the same timetable, meals and games period on all ten days.
(a) Find the average number of visits per day for each kind of day.
(b) How many times as many visits were there on an average poor-air day as on an average good-air day?
(c) Using the chapter, explain what the data suggests, and why the same timetable and meals matter for this conclusion.
(d) The principal says, 'Since the air causes the coughing, students' own habits do not matter for their health.' Evaluate this.
questions.a: (a) Poor-air days: (18 + 22 + 25 + 20 + 15) / 5 = 100 / 5 = 20 visits; good-air days: (4 + 3 + 5 + 2 + 6) / 5 = 20 / 5 = 4 visits. (b) 20 / 4 = 5 times as many. (c) Clean air is important for health: air pollution from vehicles and factories can cause problems like coughing or asthma, and the AQI tells how clean the air is. Because the timetable, meals and games were the same on all days, the air is the main thing that changed, so the extra coughing points to the polluted air. (d) The principal is only partly right: the environment matters, but the chapter says our health depends on both our environment and our lifestyle (balanced diet, activity, sleep, saying no to tobacco), so habits still matter.
s: (a) averages of 20 and 4 visits per day
(b) 5 times as many
(c) polluted air can cause coughing; other factors were the same, so the air is the likely cause
(d) habits still matter, because health depends on lifestyle as well as environment

questions.q:
Nurse Joseph at a residential school in Ooty keeps notes on three students one evening.
Asha says her throat hurts and she feels very tired; the thermometer shows 101.3 °F, a fever.
Bilal fell in the playground; his wrist is red and swollen, and he says it is painful.
Chetan says he feels dizzy; his temperature and blood pressure are normal and nothing unusual can be seen.
(a) Write one symptom that Asha has.
(b) Write one sign that Bilal has.
(c) Which student has only a symptom and no sign in the nurse's notes?
(d) The doctor in town has asked the nurse to send first any student with a measured sign of fever. Whom should she send first? Explain using the meaning of a sign.
questions.a: (a) Sore throat (throat pain) or tiredness, which she feels. (b) The swelling or redness of the wrist, which can be seen. (c) Chetan: dizziness is felt, and nothing could be seen or measured. (d) Asha: her temperature of 101.3 °F is a sign of fever because it is measured with a thermometer; Bilal's sign is swelling, not fever, and Chetan has no sign.
s: (a) one symptom of Asha: throat pain or tiredness
(b) one sign of Bilal: swelling or redness of the wrist
(c) Chetan
(d) Asha, because her high temperature is measured, which makes it a sign of fever

questions.q: What does the chapter call disease-causing organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms and protozoa?
questions.a: Pathogens: disease-causing organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms and protozoa.

questions.q: Which of these diseases is transmitted by insects such as mosquitoes?
questions.a: Malaria: it is caused by protozoa and spread by mosquitoes. Cholera spreads through contaminated water and food, while tuberculosis and chickenpox spread through the air.

questions.q:
Match each disease in Column I with its causal agent in Column II.
Column I: 1. Malaria  2. Tuberculosis  3. Ascariasis  4. Measles
Column II: A. Protozoa  B. Bacteria  C. Worms  D. Virus
questions.a: 1-A, 2-B, 3-C, 4-D: malaria is caused by protozoa, tuberculosis by bacteria, ascariasis by roundworms and measles by a virus.

questions.q:
Read the statements about diseases.
Statement I: All communicable diseases are caused by pathogens.
Statement II: Houseflies can act as vectors that spread pathogens.
Statement III: Every disease is caused by an infection.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: some diseases result from poor nutrition or an unhealthy lifestyle, such as deficiency diseases or diabetes, and are not caused by pathogens.

questions.q: True or False: Cholera and typhoid are both caused by bacteria that infect the intestine, and both spread through contaminated water and food. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Both are caused by bacteria, both have the intestine as the site of infection, and both are among the diseases spread through contaminated water and food (prevented by properly cooked food and boiled drinking water).
s: Verdict: True
Reason: both are bacterial diseases of the intestine spread through contaminated water and food

questions.q:
(a) What is a communicable disease?
(b) Name any two communicable diseases given in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A disease caused by pathogens that can spread from one person to another. (b) Any two of typhoid, dengue, flu, chickenpox, COVID-19, measles, tuberculosis, cholera, malaria, hepatitis A.
s: (a) caused by pathogens and can spread from one person to another
(b) any two correct examples

questions.q:
Answer about dengue fever.
(a) What is its causal agent?
(b) What is its site of infection?
(c) Name one preventive measure the chapter lists for dengue but not for malaria.
questions.a: (a) A virus. (b) Skin and blood. (c) Avoiding areas with still water.
s: (a) virus
(b) skin and blood
(c) avoiding areas with still water

questions.q: Rahul says: 'Hepatitis A attacks the liver, not the intestine, so it cannot spread through contaminated water and food the way cholera does.' Is he right? Explain using what the chapter says about hepatitis A.
questions.a: No, he is wrong. The chapter lists hepatitis A among the diseases spread through contaminated water and food, even though its site of infection is the liver. The site of infection does not decide the route of spread. Its preventive measures, drinking boiled water and vaccination, also show that it is caught from contaminated water.
s: Verdict: wrong
Hepatitis A is listed as spread through contaminated water and food although it infects the liver
The site of infection does not decide how a disease spreads; boiled water as its prevention supports this

questions.q:
In one week, the health room of a boys' hostel in Jodhpur records three groups of cases.
Group P: 6 boys with nasal congestion, sore throat, cough and body ache.
Group Q: 4 boys with high fever, profuse sweating and chills that come and go.
Group R: 2 boys with diarrhoea and dehydration.
The warden's inspection finds three problems: towels and handkerchiefs are shared in the bathrooms; desert coolers have stood with still water for weeks; and the drinking-water filter has been broken for ten days.
(a) Name the likely disease in Group Q and what spreads it.
(b) Name the likely disease in Group R and how it spreads.
(c) Link each of the three problems to the group of cases it most likely fed.
(d) This week the warden can repair only one problem. Choose one and justify your choice using the data.
questions.a: (a) Malaria (caused by protozoa), spread by mosquitoes. (b) Cholera, spread through contaminated water and food. (c) Shared towels and handkerchiefs: Group P (cold and influenza spread by sharing personal items); still water in the coolers: Group Q (mosquitoes breed there); broken filter: Group R (contaminated drinking water). (d) Either choice earns the mark if justified with the data, for example: empty and dry the coolers, because Group Q is larger (4 boys against 2) and malaria brings high fever; or repair the filter, because cholera causes dehydration and every boy drinks the water. Sharing towels can be stopped by a simple rule without any repair.
s: (a) malaria, spread by mosquitoes
(b) cholera, through contaminated water and food
(c) towels to P, coolers to Q, filter to R
(d) one repair chosen and justified with the numbers or seriousness of the cases

questions.q:
For each disease below, state (i) its causal agent and (ii) how it spreads: through the air, through contaminated water and food, or by insects.
(a) Chickenpox
(b) Typhoid
(c) Malaria
(d) Ascariasis
(e) Influenza
questions.a: (a) Chickenpox: virus; through the air. (b) Typhoid: bacteria; through contaminated water and food. (c) Malaria: protozoa; by insects (mosquitoes). (d) Ascariasis: worms (roundworms); through contaminated water and food. (e) Influenza: virus; through the air.
s: (a) chickenpox: virus, air
(b) typhoid: bacteria, contaminated water and food
(c) malaria: protozoa, insects (mosquitoes)
(d) ascariasis: worms, contaminated water and food
(e) influenza: virus, air

questions.q: Scurvy, anaemia and goitre are caused by a lack of specific nutrients in the diet. What are such diseases called?
questions.a: Deficiency diseases; they are also non-communicable.

questions.q: The chapter calls cancer, diabetes and asthma chronic diseases because they may often persist for a long time. For more than how long?
questions.a: More than 3 months.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Diabetes is a non-communicable disease.
Reason (R): Diabetes is becoming more common in children as well as in adults.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Diabetes is non-communicable because it is not caused by a pathogen and does not spread from one person to another; how common it is says nothing about whether it spreads.

questions.q: True or False: Scurvy, anaemia and goitre are non-communicable diseases. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. They are deficiency diseases, caused by a lack of specific nutrients in the diet and not by pathogens, so they do not spread from one person to another.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: they are deficiency diseases caused by a lack of nutrients, not by pathogens

questions.q:
(a) Name two deficiency diseases given in the chapter.
(b) Name two chronic diseases given in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Any two of scurvy, anaemia and goitre. (b) Any two of cancer, diabetes and asthma.
s: (a) any two of scurvy, anaemia, goitre
(b) any two of cancer, diabetes, asthma

questions.q:
Forty years ago, Mr Kulkarni's father in Nashik walked to work and ate home-cooked meals. Today Mr Kulkarni drives to his office, sits at a desk most of the day and often eats packaged, processed snacks. His father is now 82.
(a) Name two changes in this family that the chapter links to non-communicable diseases becoming more common in India.
(b) The father's age points to a third reason the chapter gives. What is it?
questions.a: (a) Eating more processed food, and getting less exercise. (b) People are living longer lives.
s: (a) more processed food and less exercise
(b) people living longer lives

questions.q: State three causes that, according to the chapter, often combine to make a person develop diabetes.
questions.a: Any three of: hormonal imbalances; unhealthy eating habits; lack of physical activity; being overweight or obese.
s: First cause (hormonal imbalances / unhealthy eating / lack of physical activity / overweight or obesity)
Second, different cause from the same list
Third, different cause from the same list

questions.q:
Mrs D'Souza, 52, is overweight and rarely exercises. She is always thirsty, urinates often, feels tired, and a small cut on her foot has taken weeks to heal.
(a) Which disease do these signs and symptoms point to?
(b) Name two features of her lifestyle or body that the chapter links to this disease.
(c) Her grandson asks whether he can catch it by eating from her plate. Answer him with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Diabetes (frequent urination, excessive thirst, tiredness and slow healing). (b) Lack of physical activity, and being overweight. (c) No: diabetes is non-communicable; it is not caused by a pathogen and does not spread from one person to another.
s: (a) diabetes
(b) lack of physical activity and being overweight
(c) no, because diabetes is non-communicable and does not spread between people

questions.q:
A health camp in a village near Koraput checks 120 children aged 6 to 12 and finds that 30 of them have anaemia. Of these 30 children, 12 also have worms in their stool, poor appetite and weight loss. Most families eat the same plain meal every day with few vegetables. Many children do not wash their hands before eating, and the village has no supply of boiled or filtered drinking water.
(a) What percentage of the children checked have anaemia?
(b) Anaemia caused by a lack of nutrients belongs to which group of non-communicable diseases?
(c) Which communicable disease named in the chapter can also cause anaemia, and is likely in the 12 children?
(d) A volunteer says, 'A better diet alone will end all 30 cases.' Judge her claim using the data.
questions.a: (a) 30 / 120 x 100 = 25%. (b) Deficiency diseases. (c) Ascariasis (roundworm infection), whose symptoms include worms in stool, loss of appetite, weight loss and anaemia. (d) Only partly right. A varied diet can help the 30 - 12 = 18 children whose anaemia is likely from a lack of nutrients, but the 12 with worms also need ascariasis prevented: personal hygiene, good sanitary habits, properly cooked food and boiled drinking water. So diet alone will not end all 30 cases.
s: (b) deficiency diseases
(c) ascariasis (roundworms)
(d) partly right: diet helps the 18, but the 12 with worms also need hygiene, cooked food and boiled water

questions.q:
Compare communicable and non-communicable diseases under five heads:
(a) what causes them,
(b) whether they spread from one person to another,
(c) what they are usually linked to or spread by,
(d) two examples of each,
(e) one way of preventing or managing each.
questions.a: (a) Communicable: pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, worms or protozoa); non-communicable: not caused by pathogens. (b) Communicable diseases can spread from person to person; non-communicable diseases do not. (c) Communicable: spread through air, contact, contaminated food and water, and vectors; non-communicable: usually linked to lifestyle, diet and/or environment, or to a lack of nutrients (deficiency diseases). (d) Communicable: for example typhoid, dengue, chickenpox; non-communicable: for example diabetes, cancer, asthma, scurvy. (e) Communicable: for example washing hands, boiled water, mosquito nets or vaccination; non-communicable: healthy habits such as a balanced diet and regular exercise, and for chronic diseases early diagnosis and continuous care.
s: (a) pathogens versus not caused by pathogens
(b) spread from person to person versus do not spread
(c) routes of spread versus lifestyle, diet, environment or lack of nutrients
(d) two correct examples of each
(e) one correct prevention or management for each

questions.q: What is the natural ability of our body to fight diseases called?
questions.a: Immunity; it is provided by the body's immune system.

questions.q: When did Edward Jenner discover that people who had cowpox did not get smallpox?
questions.a: In the late 1700s. (1928 is when penicillin was discovered, 1965 marks the vaccine campaign and 1979 the eradication of smallpox.)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Vaccines are curative: they treat a disease once a person is already sick with it.
Reason (R): A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise and attack harmful germs.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Vaccines are preventive, not curative: they help minimise serious diseases before they happen but do not treat someone who is already sick. R is true: a vaccine trains the immune system to recognise and attack harmful germs.

questions.q:
Match each stage of Edward Jenner's work in Column I with what happened in Column II.
Column I: 1. Observation  2. Hypothesis  3. Experimentation  4. Application
Column II: A. Mass vaccination eventually helped eradicate smallpox worldwide  B. Milkmaids who had cowpox did not catch smallpox  C. Cowpox sap was injected into a boy, who later showed no illness when exposed to smallpox  D. Content in the pus of cowpox blisters protected people from smallpox
questions.a: 1-B, 2-D, 3-C, 4-A: he observed the milkmaids, guessed that cowpox pus protected people, tested it on a boy, and mass vaccination later eradicated smallpox.

questions.q:
(a) What is acquired immunity?
(b) Name any one disease against which children are given vaccine drops or injections, as listed in the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Protection developed after exposure to a pathogen or a vaccine. (b) Any one of polio, measles, tetanus and hepatitis.
s: (a) protection developed after exposure to a pathogen or a vaccine
(b) any one of polio, measles, tetanus, hepatitis

questions.q:
In Edward Jenner's test, a boy was injected with sap from cowpox blisters and was later exposed to smallpox, but he showed no illness.
(a) What was Jenner's hypothesis?
(b) Use the idea of acquired immunity to explain why the boy did not fall ill.
questions.a: (a) That the content in the pus of cowpox blisters protected people from smallpox. (b) The cowpox sap exposed the boy's immune system to a germ related to smallpox; this trained it to recognise and fight smallpox, giving him acquired immunity (protection developed after exposure), so he stayed well.
s: (a) content in the pus of cowpox blisters protects people from smallpox
(b) exposure to the related cowpox germ trained his immune system, giving acquired immunity against smallpox

questions.q: Ritu's aunt says: 'Every vaccine is made from a whole live germ, so every vaccine gives you the disease in a mild form.' Is the claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain using how vaccines are made.
questions.a: Wrong. Vaccines are made in different ways: from weakened or dead pathogens, from inactive or harmless parts of a pathogen, or (newer vaccines) by instructing our own body cells to make a harmless part of the germ. They train the immune system without causing the disease; for example, the tetanus shot contains an inactivated bacterial toxin that builds protection without causing tetanus.
s: Verdict: wrong
Vaccines are made from weakened or dead pathogens, harmless parts, or by making body cells produce a harmless part
They build protection without causing the disease, as the inactivated toxin in the tetanus shot shows

questions.q:
A chickenpox case is reported in the Bose household. The family:
Grandmother: had chickenpox as a child and recovered.
Anu, 10: was given the chickenpox vaccine two years ago.
Rahul, 15: has had chickenpox for two days, with mild fever, itchy rashes and blisters.
Baby Tia, 3 months: has not been vaccinated.
(a) Who has acquired immunity from an earlier infection, and who from a vaccine?
(b) Rahul's uncle wants him to get the vaccine now so that his blisters clear faster. Explain why this will not work.
(c) Using the chapter's preventive measures for chickenpox, say what the family should do about Rahul.
(d) Explain how Anu being vaccinated also helps protect Tia.
questions.a: (a) Grandmother, from her earlier infection; Anu, from the vaccine. (b) Vaccines are preventive, not curative: they do not treat a disease once someone is already sick. (c) Keep Rahul completely isolated from the others (especially Tia) and have him cover his mouth and nose. (d) Getting vaccinated protects not only you but also the people around you: Anu is unlikely to catch chickenpox, so she will not carry it to Tia.
s: (a) grandmother from infection, Anu from the vaccine
(b) vaccines prevent disease but do not cure someone already sick
(c) complete isolation of Rahul and covering the mouth and nose
(d) a vaccinated person does not pass the disease on, so vaccination protects people around her

questions.q:
A school in Indore has 800 students. Before a measles vaccination camp, 560 of them had already received the measles vaccine. On camp day, 200 more students were vaccinated, but some were absent. The camp now has doses left for exactly 30 more children. A nearby anganwadi has 30 young children, none of whom has received the measles vaccine.
(a) What percentage of the school's students were vaccinated before the camp?
(b) What percentage are vaccinated after camp day, and how many students are still not vaccinated?
(c) A week later one unvaccinated student, Kunal, falls ill with measles. Should he now be given a dose to cure him? Give a reason.
(d) Should the 30 doses go to the school's unvaccinated students or to the anganwadi children? Decide, and justify with the numbers.
questions.a: (a) 560 / 800 x 100 = 70%. (b) 560 + 200 = 760 vaccinated; 760 / 800 x 100 = 95%; 800 - 760 = 40 still not vaccinated. (c) No: vaccines are preventive, not curative, so a dose will not treat Kunal's measles; he needs a doctor and isolation. (d) Either decision earns the mark if justified with the numbers, for example: the anganwadi, because 0 of its 30 children are protected while 95% of the school already is; or the school, because measles is now inside the school and its unvaccinated students are exposed. Vaccines protect people of all ages, and getting vaccinated also protects the people around you.
s: (b) 95%, with 40 students not vaccinated
(c) no, because vaccines are preventive, not curative
(d) a clear decision justified with the coverage numbers (0% at the anganwadi or the exposed unvaccinated students)

questions.q:
At a vaccination camp in a town in Bihar, a health worker hears five remarks. For each, say whether it is correct, and correct it if it is not, using the chapter.
(a) 'Vaccines are only for babies; adults and old people do not need them.'
(b) 'Some vaccines are made from dead pathogens.'
(c) 'If I get vaccinated, only I benefit; nobody else is protected.'
(d) 'A vaccine can cure my son's typhoid now that he has it.'
(e) 'Nobody checks whether vaccines are safe.'
questions.a: (a) Not correct: vaccines protect people of all ages, from infants to the elderly. (b) Correct: vaccines can be made from weakened or dead pathogens, or from inactive or harmless parts of a pathogen. (c) Not correct: getting vaccinated protects you and also the people around you, and vaccines reduce the spread of infections. (d) Not correct: vaccines are preventive, not curative; they do not treat a disease once someone is already sick (for a bacterial disease like typhoid a doctor may give antibiotics). (e) Not correct: scientists and doctors carefully test vaccines for safety.
s: (a) not correct: vaccines protect all ages, infants to the elderly
(b) correct: some vaccines are made from dead (or weakened) pathogens
(c) not correct: vaccination also protects the people around you
(d) not correct: vaccines prevent, they do not cure an existing disease
(e) not correct: scientists and doctors carefully test vaccines for safety

questions.q: According to the chapter, what do antibiotics kill?
o: The bacteria that cause an infection
The viruses that cause an infection
Every kind of pathogen, including viruses
questions.a: The bacteria that cause an infection; antibiotics do not work against viruses or diseases caused by protozoa.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Antibiotics cannot cure dengue fever.
Reason (R): Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections, and dengue is caused by a virus.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: dengue is a viral disease, and antibiotics do not work against viruses.

questions.q:
Read the statements about antibiotics.
Statement I: Antibiotics work against viruses as well as bacteria.
Statement II: Fleming noticed that a mould on a discarded petri dish stopped bacteria from growing.
Statement III: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria can spread through soil in a crop field via manure or animal faeces.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: antibiotics work only against bacterial infections, not against viruses or diseases caused by protozoa.

questions.q: True or False: When antibiotics kill the bacteria causing an illness, they leave all the other bacteria in the body untouched. Give the verdict and correct the statement if needed.
questions.a: False. When antibiotics kill the bacteria causing illness, they also kill good bacteria that protect the body from infection.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: antibiotics also kill the good bacteria that protect the body from infection

questions.q:
(a) What is antibiotic resistance?
(b) State one effect it has on common infections.
questions.a: (a) A phenomenon where bacteria that were earlier killed by a given antibiotic survive and multiply despite treatment with that antibiotic. (b) Any one: it makes common infections harder to treat; it increases the risk of complications, prolonged illness and even death.
s: (a) bacteria once killed by an antibiotic now survive and multiply despite it
(b) infections become harder to treat, or more risk of complications, prolonged illness or death

questions.q:
Ms Gupta's son has influenza. Without asking a doctor, she gives him some antibiotic tablets left over from his father's treatment last year.
(a) Will the tablets cure his influenza? Give a reason.
(b) State two ways in which her action goes against the chapter's advice on using antibiotics wisely.
(c) Explain how such use can harm people later.
questions.a: (a) No: influenza is caused by a virus, and antibiotics work only against bacteria. (b) Any two: the antibiotic was not prescribed by a doctor; it is being taken when not required; the dose and the duration are not the correct ones for him. (c) Taking antibiotics when they are not required helps bacteria become resistant, so later the antibiotic may stop working and infections become harder to treat.
s: (a) no, influenza is viral and antibiotics act only on bacteria
(b) two breaches: no prescription, not required, wrong dose or duration
(c) such use leads to antibiotic resistance, making infections harder to treat later

questions.q:
A hospital laboratory tests 100 samples of the same kind of disease-causing bacteria against antibiotic X every few years. Antibiotic X killed the bacteria in 95 samples in 2016, in 80 samples in 2020 and in 55 samples in 2024.
(a) Find the number of samples in which the bacteria survived in each of the three years.
(b) Name the phenomenon this trend shows, and say what it means.
(c) Give two human actions, from the chapter, that could have caused this trend.
questions.a: (a) 2016: 100 - 95 = 5; 2020: 100 - 80 = 20; 2024: 100 - 55 = 45. (b) Antibiotic resistance: bacteria that were earlier killed by antibiotic X now survive and multiply despite it. (c) Any two: taking antibiotics when they are not required; taking an incomplete dose; giving antibiotics to animals that do not need them, from which resistant bacteria reach people.
s: (a) 5, 20 and 45 samples survived
(b) antibiotic resistance, with its meaning
(c) two causes: use when not required, incomplete dose, or unneeded use in animals

questions.q:
A village health committee near Mysuru wants to slow the spread of antibiotic resistance and has money for only two of three plans.
Plan P: a door-to-door drive telling families to take antibiotics only with a doctor's prescription and to finish the full course.
Plan Q: training dairy farmers not to inject antibiotics into cattle that are not ill.
Plan R: daily cleaning of hospital surfaces.
A survey shows that 40% of families stopped their last antibiotic course early, 60% of dairy farmers inject healthy cattle with antibiotics, and the village has no hospital (patients go to the town).
(a) Explain how the habit Plan P targets leads to resistance.
(b) Explain a route by which the habit Plan Q targets can bring resistant bacteria to people.
(c) Why would Plan R do the least good in this village?
(d) Which two plans should the committee choose? Justify with the survey data.
questions.a: (a) Taking antibiotics without need or leaving a course incomplete lets bacteria develop resistance; the resistant bacteria then grow and spread. (b) Bacteria in the cattle develop resistance; they reach people through animal food products, or through manure in crop fields and then the crop produce. (c) Resistant bacteria spread in hospitals through dirty surfaces and between patients, but the village has no hospital, so this plan does not touch a local source. (d) Plans P and Q: 40% of families misuse antibiotic courses and 60% of farmers give antibiotics to healthy cattle, so both target large local sources of resistance.
s: (a) incomplete or unneeded use lets bacteria develop resistance
(b) resistance in animal bacteria reaches people via animal food products or manure and crops
(c) the village has no hospital, so hospital-surface cleaning tackles no local source
(d) choose P and Q, using the 40% and 60% figures

questions.q:
The science club of a Jaipur school asks 50 families about antibiotics in the past year. Of these, 18 families bought antibiotics from a chemist without a doctor's prescription, 12 families stopped an antibiotic course as soon as the patient felt better, and 9 families gave antibiotics for a cold or flu.
(a) What percentage of the families bought antibiotics without a prescription?
(b) Which of the three habits uses antibiotics against an illness caused by a virus?
(c) Why does that habit not help the patient?
(d) The club can speak about only one habit in its assembly talk. Which one would you choose? Justify using the numbers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 18 / 50 x 100 = 36%. (b) Giving antibiotics for a cold or flu. (c) Cold and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only against bacteria, so they cannot cure it; such use only adds to resistance. (d) For example, buying without a prescription, because it is the most common habit (36%, against 24% for stopping early and 18% for colds) and the chapter says antibiotics should be used only when prescribed by a doctor. Stopping courses early is also accepted if justified, since an incomplete dose helps resistance develop.
s: (b) giving antibiotics for a cold or flu
(c) cold and flu are viral and antibiotics act only on bacteria
(d) one habit chosen and justified with the percentages and the chapter's advice

questions.q:
Ravi and Meena, cousins in Chennai, fall ill in the same week of the monsoon. Ravi has typhoid; Meena has dengue.
(a) Name the causal agent of each disease.
(b) Can an antibiotic treat each of them? Give a reason for each.
(c) Give one preventive measure from the chapter for each disease.
(d) On day 3 of a 7-day antibiotic course, Ravi feels better and wants to stop. Explain the risk.
(e) Meena's family asks a chemist for antibiotics 'just in case', without a prescription. Judge this request.
questions.a: (a) Typhoid: bacteria; dengue: virus. (b) Ravi: yes, a doctor may give antibiotics because typhoid is a bacterial infection. Meena: no, because antibiotics do not work against viruses. (c) Typhoid: personal hygiene and good sanitary habits, properly cooked food and boiled drinking water, or vaccination. Dengue: mosquito nets and repellents, long-sleeved clothes, controlling mosquito breeding, or avoiding areas with still water. (d) Leaving the course incomplete can let surviving bacteria develop antibiotic resistance, so the antibiotic may stop working and the resistant bacteria can spread to others. (e) The request is wrong: antibiotics should be used only when prescribed by a doctor; they cannot help dengue, and taking them when not required adds to antibiotic resistance.
s: (a) typhoid bacteria, dengue virus
(b) antibiotic can help Ravi (bacterial) but not Meena (viral)
(c) one correct preventive measure for each disease
(d) an incomplete course lets surviving bacteria develop resistance
(e) wrong: only with a prescription; useless for a virus and adds to resistance
